title: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
hook: the lord who raises and tends every world, not just yours

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Fatiha, the opening, and its first verse, a doorway made of a name. Your line was in the name of the merciful. Did a gentle first sentence help? Day seven.

A week ago this started with one word. Salaam. Since then: bismillah, alhamdulillah, inshallah, the five pillars, and the opening of a prayer. Two of those words were already waiting inside that prayer. Bismillah is its first verse. And alhamdulillah is the very first word of the second. So today, as the week closes, the week comes back to meet us. Verse two takes the thank-you you learned on day three and points it somewhere enormous. Not at your day. At every world there is.
screen: `A WEEK OF WORDS.` → `BISMILLAH: VERSE ONE.` → `ALHAMDULILLAH: VERSE TWO.`

segments.voice: Verse two, in Pickthall's words: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” In Arabic, al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin. The first half is your day-three word, alhamdulillah. The small al- at the front makes it all praise, every kind, belonging to God. Now the new word. Rabb. English usually says Lord, and that's right, but it's thin. Rabb is the one who owns and the one who looks after. Classical commentators explain it with the picture of raising something: bringing a child, or a seedling, along step by step until it's grown. So a rabb isn't a distant owner with paperwork. It's the one who feeds, shelters and brings you up. And then: al-'alamin. The worlds. Not the world, the worlds, plural. Commentators have listed people, angels, animals, every kind of created thing; some say each kind is a world of its own. The ant colony under the sidewalk. The deep sea. The inside of a stranger's life on the train. All of it, the verse says, is being raised and tended by one Rabb. A hadith qudsi, a saying of God reported by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and recorded by Muslim, adds a detail. It describes al-Fatiha as a conversation. When someone praying says this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me. So the thank-you from day three isn't said into empty air. In the prayer, it's heard, and answered. Two verses down, five to go.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE.` · `RABB — THE ONE WHO RAISES.` · `AL-'ALAMIN — THE WORLDS, PLURAL.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.` · then, large: `EVERY WORLD IS TENDED.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. First breath: your own world. One thing in it that's being looked after, even today. Second breath: a world that isn't yours. A bird, a stranger, a field somewhere you'll never see. Third breath: hold both at once. If you want, the Arabic rides out on the last one: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin.
Rabb. Lord: the one who owns, raises and looks after, here the Lord of all the worlds. Seventh word, and a full week on your strand.
Your line: every world is tended. Today, notice one small world that isn't yours, a plant on a windowsill, a neighbor's routine, and whatever keeps it going. A week, done. Day seven.

howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and many say alhamdulillah, its opening word, many times a day. Rabb is also the word Muslims use in many personal prayers, often as Rabbi, my Lord, or Rabbana, our Lord.

God answers: My servant has praised Me.

original.note: Arabic: lord, master, the one who raises and looks after. in al-Fatiha: rabbi l-'alamin, Lord of the Worlds.

trapdoor: what you thought: "Lord" — a title, like a king's.
what it means: the one who owns and looks after, raising every world along.
what a scholar hears: commentators gloss rabb with tarbiya, bringing a thing gradually to completion; al-'alamin, plural of 'alam, is read as every class of creation.

notes: Rabb explained through tarbiya (raising step by step to completion) follows classical commentators such as al-Baydawi; lexicographers differ on whether tarbiya shares rabb's root. The script says 'commentators explain it with the picture of raising'; confirm.
Al-'alamin as every class of creation (people, angels, animals, jinn): a common tafsir reading among several. Confirm.
Sahih Muslim 395 (hadith qudsi, 'I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant') cited from memory; the script paraphrases. Please confirm the number.
